title: Basic Cooking & Workstation Skills
subtitle: Heat moves three ways — and water stops at 100 degrees.
objectives: Name the three ways heat moves
Explain why you cannot brown food in water
Run a workstation in the right order

cards.title: Cooking is heat, moved three ways
cards.text: Every method you will ever use is one of three ways of moving heat into food. Knowing which one tells you what the method can and cannot do.

cards.title: Conduction, convection, radiation
cards.text: Three mechanisms, and every method is one of them.
points: **Conduction** — touching. Pan to food.
**Convection** — a moving fluid. Boiling water, oven air.
**Radiation** — straight from a hot source. A grill above food.
**Most real cooking** uses two at once.

cards.title: You run the workstation
cards.text: Pick the first move. Each wrong order shows what it would cost.

question.explain: The moving water carries the heat.

cards.title: Water stops at 100°C
cards.text: This is the single most useful fact in cooking.
points: **Water cannot get hotter than 100°C** in an open pan.
**Browning needs more than about 140°C.**
**So you cannot brown anything in water.** Ever.
**Oil can reach 180°C and above.** That is why frying browns.

question.text: Why can you not brown meat in boiling water?
options: Water cannot exceed 100°C and browning needs about 140°C
question.explain: The ceiling is physical, not a technique problem.

cards.title: Dry heat and moist heat
cards.text: The family tells you what you will get.
points: **Dry heat:** fry, sauté, grill, roast. Browning, crust, flavour.
**Moist heat:** boil, simmer, steam, poach. Tender, no crust.
**Braising uses both:** brown first, then liquid.
**That is why adobo is browned** before the vinegar goes in.

cards.title: Why a pan has a thick base
cards.text: The base is a heat spreader, exactly like the one under a processor.
points: **Thin metal makes hot spots** straight above the flame.
**A thick base conducts sideways** before it conducts up.
**Same job as a heatsink.**
**Aluminium in both**, for the same reason.

cards.title: Same chicken, two pans
cards.alt: Chicken browning deep gold in oil beside the same chicken simmering pale in water
cards.text: Oil reaches 180°C and browns it. Water stops at 100°C and never will.

question.text: You cannot brown food in boiling water because…
options: water cannot pass 100°C and browning needs about 140°C
question.explain: The ceiling is physical. No technique gets round it.

cards.title: Oil fire: never water
cards.text: Water on burning oil is the most dangerous thing in a kitchen, and the reason is physics.
points: **Water hits oil above 300°C** and flashes to steam instantly.
**It expands about 1,700 times**, throwing burning oil upward.
**Turn off the heat. Cover with a lid.**
**Same rule as an engine bay fire.** Smother, do not spray.

cards.title: A simmer is not a boil
cards.text: Pacing matters as much in a pan as in a round.
points: **A boil is a rolling, breaking surface.**
**A simmer is a few lazy bubbles.**
**Boiling meat makes it tough.** Simmering makes it tender.
**Lower and longer wins** in both.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Conduction touches, convection moves, radiation beams.
Water stops at 100°C, so nothing browns in it.
Dry heat browns; moist heat tenderises; braising does both.
Oil fire: heat off, lid on. Never water.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 7 TLE. The week is built on physics rather than technique lists: three heat-transfer mechanisms, then the single most useful fact in cooking, which is that water cannot exceed 100°C while browning needs about 140°C. That one fact explains why nothing browns in a pan of water, why frying browns, and why braising starts dry. The oil-fire lens is the most important safety content in the subject and is given with the reason — water flashing to steam and expanding roughly 1,700 times — because a rule with a mechanism survives panic better than a rule without one. The thick-base pan is linked to a heatsink, which is the same job in the same metal.
discussion: Ask which of the three mechanisms each method uses.
Ask why you cannot brown anything in water.
Ask what to do about a pan of burning oil, and why not water.
Ask him to show the difference between a boil and a simmer.
extension: Have him brown half an onion in oil and simmer the other half in water, then compare.
Have him find the thickest-based pan in the house and explain why it is thick.
misconceptions: "Boiling long enough will brown it." The ceiling is 100°C.
"Water puts out a fire." Not an oil fire — it throws it upward.
"A simmer is a gentle boil." A few lazy bubbles, not a rolling surface.
